Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning

Anutam Srinivasan Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, School of Electrical & Computer Engineering, {asrinivasan350,spanse30}@gatech.edu    Siddhant Panse Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, School of Electrical & Computer Engineering, {asrinivasan350,spanse30}@gatech.edu    Glen Chou Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, Schools of Cybersecurity & Privacy, Aerospace Engineering, chou@gatech.edu
Abstract

Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.

I Introduction

Robots operating in unstructured environments must act safely despite uncertainty in their dynamics and surroundings. Robust control is one approach to achieve this, providing worst-case guarantees by treating uncertainty as persistently adversarial, propagating reachable tubes over admissible uncertainty, and tightening constraints accordingly. While this is appropriate for irreducible aleatoric uncertainty, it can be overly conservative for epistemic uncertainty arising from unknown but learnable physical parameters such as mass, friction, wind, or motor damage. Because this structured uncertainty can be reduced through interaction, robust adaptive control can become less conservative as parameter estimates improve online. As data is collected and parameter uncertainty shrinks, controllers can safely exploit the reduced uncertainty to improve performance. Moreover, because the rate of learning depends on how informative the chosen trajectory is, control actions can directly influence future parameter uncertainty, creating a tradeoff between performance, robustness, and information gathering.

However, designing robust adaptive controllers for robotics remains an open problem, with two central challenges. First, synthesizing adaptive controllers while jointly reasoning about estimation error, aleatoric uncertainty, and parametric uncertainty is computationally expensive for long-horizon, high-dimensional nonlinear systems, yet practical robotic systems require real-time learning, verification, and controller adaptation. Second, many existing methods update parameter estimates online but plan using the current parameter uncertainty set, incorporating newly learned information only reactively after measurements are collected. As a result, they cannot exploit guaranteed future uncertainty reduction during planning and may produce unnecessarily large reachable tubes even along informative trajectories. For example, a drone traversing an uncertain but learnable wind field should be able to plan knowing that it can measure, estimate, and compensate for the wind during execution. Ignoring this future learning can degrade performance or prevent task completion, while also leading to myopic planning that fails to seek informative trajectories that accelerate uncertainty reduction. Addressing these challenges requires jointly modeling the state and parameter-estimate dynamics while efficiently forecasting the worst-case learning guaranteed under all admissible uncertainties.

In this work, we close these gaps with A-SLS, a scalable robust adaptive policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for future learning during planning. Building on system-level synthesis (SLS) [1], we augment the physical state with the online parameter estimate so that estimator evolution becomes part of the closed-loop dynamics. We propagate bounded parameter uncertainty and parameter-estimate shifts over the planning horizon, while adaptive SLS responses preserve correlations among process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tighter reachable tubes. Crucially, this enables assured future learning: for each candidate trajectory, we forecast the parameter uncertainty guaranteed to remain after future observations, allowing the optimizer to exploit worst-case future tube contraction without assuming favorable measurements. Because informativeness depends on the trajectory, the same formulation can also favor motions that accelerate uncertainty reduction. Finally, the structured SLS policy class admits efficient parallel reachability and robust constraint tightening, enabling GPU-parallel optimization for long-horizon, high-dimensional nonlinear systems. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate learning-aware robust adaptive control as an SLS problem that augments the state with the online parameter estimate, returning policies that adapt to online data while remaining robust to residual uncertainty.

  • •

    We derive reachable sets that preserve correlations between disturbances, parameter error, and estimate shifts, enabling tightened robust tubes that account for and guarantee future learning. These information-sensitive tubes also enable planning that favors informative trajectories that reduce uncertainty and improve performance.

  • •

    We develop a GPU-parallel solver that enables real-time long-horizon control on high-DoF nonlinear systems.

  • •

    We evaluate safety, tube tightness, parameter learning, active information gathering, and scalability on high-dimensional nonlinear robotic systems and hardware.

II Related Work

Classic robust adaptive control [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] establishes stability guarantees under disturbances and parametric uncertainty. Recent work extends these ideas to nonlinear and unmatched uncertainty using contraction theory [7, 8, 9, 10] and ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}-LPV control [11]. Other approaches develop SLS-based robust control under parametric uncertainty [12] and robust adaptive control for linear systems [13]. While these methods provide strong stability guarantees, they generally do not optimize long-horizon constrained trajectories or anticipate how planned actions reduce uncertainty; contraction-based approaches also require challenging metric synthesis and online geodesic computation. In contrast, our method uses SLS for robust adaptive nonlinear trajectory optimization, coupling closed-loop reachability with guaranteed future learning and real-time GPU-parallel synthesis.

Other methods incorporate adaptation into safety-critical control. Adaptive and robust-adaptive control barrier functions (CBFs) provide forward-invariance guarantees under parametric uncertainty [14, 15, 16], with later applications to robotics [17, 18]. Many reduce online control to small QPs or impose Lyapunov conditions within MPC. However, synthesizing adaptive CBFs/CLFs can be challenging, and these methods typically provide pointwise invariance or stability guarantees without explicitly planning trajectories to improve parameter learning. Our approach instead couples closed-loop reachability and planning through shared uncertainty sources affecting physical states and future parameter estimates, yielding tighter robust tubes while making information gathering part of the trajectory optimization.

Robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) combines online model learning with constrained planning. Early work used conservative constraint tightenings or separate robust safety and learned performance models [19, 20]. Set-membership identification was later integrated with robust MPC for linear [21] and nonlinear systems [22, 23], with extensions addressing convergence [24], safety certification [25], ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} adaptation [26], contraction [27], and distributed control [28]. However, most methods exploit learning only after uncertainty updates are observed rather than anticipating guaranteed future estimator evolution, and can be computationally demanding online. Our adaptive SLS formulation instead jointly propagates parameter-estimation and disturbance dynamics, preserves their correlations for tighter tubes, and enables real-time GPU-parallel synthesis.

Finally, dual and active-learning MPC recognize that control affects both task execution and future model quality [29]. Persistent-excitation constraints can promote parameter convergence in RAMPC [30], while [31] embeds predicted set-membership updates in linear MPC for informative exploration. These methods closely align with our planning-to-learn objective. However, persistent excitation is an indirect proxy for task-relevant uncertainty reduction, while exact future set-membership reasoning can be expensive and difficult to scale. Our method instead optimizes worst-case parameter-estimation dynamics within a scalable SLS framework, exploiting assured future tube contraction while retaining robust nonlinear constraints and GPU-parallel computation for long-horizon, high-dimensional systems.

Directly solving (2) is typically intractable [32]. Thus, we instead optimize a nominal state-control trajectory and robust tracking controller, perform closed-loop reachability around the trajectory, and enforce constraints over the resulting reachable set. We formulate this as an SLS problem [1], solved using GPUSLS [32] and GPUSLS-LEO [33].

System Level Synthesis (SLS): SLS is a robust controller synthesis framework. Specifically, SLS optimizes causal feedback gains to track a reference trajectory. For the following uncertain LTV system,

xk+1=Ak​xk+Bk​uk+Fk​wk,x_{k+1}=A_{k}x_{k}+B_{k}u_{k}+F_{k}w_{k}, (3)

the closed-loop control input is

uk=vk+Δ​uk=vk+∑j=0k−1𝚽k,ju​Fj​wj,u_{k}=v_{k}+\Delta u_{k}=v_{k}+\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{u}}_{k,j}F_{j}w_{j}, (4)

where vk∈ℝnuv_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{u}}} is the nominal control, Δ​uk\Delta u_{k} is the feedback correction, and 𝚽k,ju∈ℝnu×nx\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{u}}_{k,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{u}}\times{n_{x}}} maps each past disturbance Fj​wjF_{j}w_{j} to the control input. Under this policy, the closed-loop state response is

xk=zk+Δ​xk=zk+∑j=0k−1𝚽k,jx​Fj​wj,z0=x¯0,x_{k}=z_{k}+\Delta x_{k}=z_{k}+\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{x}}_{k,j}F_{j}w_{j},\qquad z_{0}=\bar{x}_{0}, (5)

where zk∈ℝnxz_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}} is the nominal state, Δ​xk\Delta x_{k} is the state deviation, and 𝚽k,jx∈ℝnx×nx\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{x}}_{k,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{x}}\times{n_{x}}} maps disturbance Fj​wjF_{j}w_{j} to its effect on xkx_{k}. We set 𝚽j+1,jx=Inx\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{x}}_{j+1,j}=I_{{n_{x}}} and propagate 𝚽k+1,jx=Ak​𝚽k,jx+Bk​𝚽k,ju\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{x}}_{k+1,j}=A_{k}\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{x}}_{k,j}+B_{k}\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{u}}_{k,j}, for all j∈[N]j\in[N] and k∈[j+1,N−1]k\in[j+1,N-1]. For nonlinear systems with nominal dynamics zk+1=f⁡(zk,vk)z_{k+1}=f(z_{k},v_{k}), we construct the LTV system in (3) by linearizing about the nominal trajectory:

Ak:=∂f∂x|(zk,vk),Bk:=∂f∂u|(zk,vk),Fk:=F⁡(zk).\textstyle A_{k}:=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\big|_{(z_{k},v_{k})},\ \ B_{k}:=\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\big|_{(z_{k},v_{k})},\ \ F_{k}:=F(z_{k}). (6)

Taylor models [32] provide linearization error bounds (LEBs) that can be efficiently computed on the GPU [34] and incorporated as an additional bounded disturbance by replacing Fk​wkF_{k}w_{k} with Fk​wk+Fknl​wknlF_{k}w_{k}+F^{\textrm{nl}}_{k}w^{\textrm{nl}}_{k}, where Fknl​wknlF^{\textrm{nl}}_{k}w^{\textrm{nl}}_{k} captures the linearization error, with wknl∈ℬ∞nxw^{\textrm{nl}}_{k}\in\mathcal{B}^{{n_{x}}}_{\infty} [33].

Problem Statement (Learning-Aware Robust Adaptive Control): Given the uncertain nonlinear system (1), initial state x¯0\bar{x}_{0}, parameter estimate θ^0\hat{\theta}_{0}, uncertainty set Θ0\Theta_{0}, bounded disturbance w∈ℬ∞nxw\in\mathcal{B}^{{n_{x}}}_{\infty}, horizon NN, and constraints gkg_{k} and gNg_{N}, our goal is to solve the RANOCP (2) by jointly planning a nominal state-control trajectory and synthesizing a causal adaptive policy π\pi. Using observed transition residuals rkr_{k}, we update the parameter estimate θ^k\hat{\theta}_{k} online while bounding the future uncertainty sets Θk\Theta_{k} a priori. The policy must minimize the control objective while robustly satisfying all constraints for every admissible parameter and disturbance realization. Notably, planning accounts for the worst-case future parameter uncertainty induced by measurements along the planned trajectory, allowing predicted reachable tubes to exploit guaranteed future learning rather than treating the current parameter uncertainty set as fixed over the horizon.

IV Methodology

In this section, we present the components of our adaptive SLS formulation (A-SLS) used to plan with guaranteed future learning. We first derive the parameter-estimation (Sec. IV-A) and uncertainty-update dynamics (Sec. IV-B), then embed them into SLS to construct correlation-preserving reachable sets (Sec. IV-C) and robust constraint tightenings (Sec. IV-D). We then extend to nonlinear dynamics and discuss the resulting robust-adaptive optimization problem (Sec. IV-E).

IV-A Parameter Estimation Dynamics

We begin with the parametric LTV dynamics

xt+1=At​xt+Bt​ut+Et​θ+Ft​wt,x_{t+1}=A_{t}x_{t}+B_{t}u_{t}+E_{t}\theta+F_{t}w_{t}, (7)

where Et∈ℝnx×nθE_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{x}}\times{n_{\theta}}} is the parameter sensitivity matrix describing how θ\theta affects the dynamics. To adapt the controller, we estimate unknown parameters from observed state transitions. Given the applied control utu_{t} and measured successor state xt+1x_{t+1}, the only unknown quantities in (7) are θ\theta and wtw_{t}. To mitigate the effects of noisy measurements on estimation accuracy, we introduce a binary diagonal measurement gate Ct∈ℝnx×nxC_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{x}}\times{n_{x}}} that selects the state measurement channels used for parameter estimation. We then define

Ht:=Ct​Et=Ut​Σt​Vt⊤,Ht,ϵ†=Vt​Σt,ϵ†​Ut⊤,H_{t}:=C_{t}E_{t}=U_{t}\Sigma_{t}V_{t}^{\top},\quad H_{t,\epsilon}^{\dagger}=V_{t}\Sigma_{t,\epsilon}^{\dagger}U_{t}^{\top}, (8)

where Ht∈ℝnx×nθH_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{x}}\times{n_{\theta}}} is the gated parameter sensitivity and Ut​Σt​Vt⊤U_{t}\Sigma_{t}V_{t}^{\top} is its singular value decomposition (SVD). The SVD identifies which directions in parameter space are observable through the selected measurements. However, inverting small singular values can amplify disturbance noise. To avoid this, we define the truncated pseudoinverse:

[Σt,ϵ†]i​i={σt,i−1,σt,i≥ϵt,0,σt,i<ϵt,​ϵt=max⁡{ϵabs,ϵrel​σt,1},[\Sigma_{t,\epsilon}^{\dagger}]_{ii}=\begin{cases}\sigma_{t,i}^{-1},&\sigma_{t,i}\geq\epsilon_{t},\\ 0,&\sigma_{t,i}<\epsilon_{t},\end{cases}\,\epsilon_{t}=\max\{\epsilon_{\mathrm{abs}},\epsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\sigma_{t,1}\}, (9)

where ϵt\epsilon_{t}, ϵabs\epsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}, and ϵrel\epsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} determine which singular values are inverted [35, 36]. This allows parameter estimation even when some components of θ\theta are unobservable through HtH_{t}. We then define the gated measurement map Πt∈ℝnθ×nθ\Pi_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\theta}}\times{n_{\theta}}} and measurement uncertainty map Wt∈ℝnθ×nxW_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\theta}}\times{n_{x}}}:

Πt:=Ht,ϵ†​Ht,Wt:=Ht,ϵ†​Ct​Ft.\Pi_{t}:=H_{t,\epsilon}^{\dagger}H_{t},\,\quad W_{t}:=H_{t,\epsilon}^{\dagger}C_{t}F_{t}. (10)

Here, Πt\Pi_{t} projects onto the retained observable parameter directions, while WtW_{t} captures how disturbances propagate into the parameter measurement. Thus, applying the truncated pseudoinverse to the gated transition residual rtr_{t} yields

θ~t+1=Ht,ϵ†​Ct​(xt+1−At​xt−Bt​ut)⏟rt=Πt​θ+Wt​wt.\tilde{\theta}_{t+1}=H_{t,\epsilon}^{\dagger}\underbrace{C_{t}\left(x_{t+1}-A_{t}x_{t}-B_{t}u_{t}\right)}_{r_{t}}=\Pi_{t}\theta+W_{t}w_{t}. (11)

Hence, θ~t+1\tilde{\theta}_{t+1} provides a noisy measurement of the observable component of θ\theta, which we use to update the parameter estimate and its uncertainty set.

IV-B Bounded Set Update

Using the parameter measurement model of Sec. IV-A, we now develop a set-valued estimation update that propagates bounded parameter uncertainty while accounting for newly observed information. Since the parameter-estimation error evolves affinely under bounded disturbances and zonotopes are closed under linear transformations and Minkowski sums, the initially zonotopic parameter uncertainty set Θ0\Theta_{0} admits a zonotopic outer approximation at every future timestep. Specifically, given the uncertainty set Θt:=θ^t⊕Gt​ℬ∞pt\Theta_{t}:=\hat{\theta}_{t}\oplus G_{t}\mathcal{B}^{p_{t}}_{\infty}, where θ^t\hat{\theta}_{t} is the current parameter estimate and GtG_{t} contains ptp_{t} generators, we update the zonotope center and generators as

θ^t+1\displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{t+1} =θ^t+Kt​(θ~t+1−Πt​θ^t)\displaystyle=\hat{\theta}_{t}+K_{t}\left(\tilde{\theta}_{t+1}-\Pi_{t}\hat{\theta}_{t}\right) (12)
Gt+1\displaystyle G_{t+1} =[(Inθ−Kt​Πt)​GtKt​Wt],\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}(I_{{n_{\theta}}}-K_{t}\Pi_{t})G_{t}&K_{t}W_{t}\end{bmatrix}, (13)

where Kt∈ℝnθ×nθK_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\theta}}\times{n_{\theta}}} is the Kalman gain. The center update incorporates newly observed parameter information, while the generator update propagates residual parameter uncertainty and measurement disturbances and is efficient to compute online, ensuring that Θt+1\Theta_{t+1} contains the true parameter, i.e., θ∈Θt+1\theta\in\Theta_{t+1}, for all admissible disturbances [37]. Since Gt+1G_{t+1} determines the parameter uncertainty in Θt+1\Theta_{t+1}, we minimize the Frobenius norm of (13) as a surrogate for zonotope volume by choosing

Kt=Gt​Gt⊤​Πt⊤​(Πt​Gt​Gt⊤​Πt⊤+Wt​Wt⊤)†.K_{t}=G_{t}G_{t}^{\top}\Pi_{t}^{\top}\left(\Pi_{t}G_{t}G_{t}^{\top}\Pi_{t}^{\top}+W_{t}W_{t}^{\top}\right)^{\dagger}. (14)

Since each update in (13) adds nxn_{x} additional disturbance generators, the number of generators grows by nxn_{x} at each stage. To maintain tractability, Girard reduction can replace the resulting zonotope with a lower-order outer approximation, limiting memory growth [38]. To prevent the uncertainty bound from increasing in any parameter dimension, we first compute KtK_{t} from (14) and compare the row-wise ℓ1\ell_{1} norms ‖Gt+1‖1,r\|G_{t+1}\|_{1,\mathrm{r}} and ‖Gt‖1,r\|G_{t}\|_{1,\mathrm{r}}, which give the uncertainty radii for individual parameters. If an entry increases, we set the corresponding row of KtK_{t} to zero and recompute the update. This leaves that dimension’s uncertainty radius unchanged, guaranteeing nonincreasing coordinate-wise uncertainty while preserving containment of the true parameter. The resulting parameter uncertainty set is Θt+1=θ^t+1⊕Gt+1​ℬ∞pt+1\Theta_{t+1}=\hat{\theta}_{t+1}\oplus G_{t+1}\mathcal{B}^{p_{t+1}}_{\infty}.

Although the future set center θ^t+1\hat{\theta}_{t+1} is unknown at planning time, WtW_{t} in (10) can be computed a priori along a candidate trajectory. This enables us to evaluate KtK_{t} using (14) and recursively propagate (13) to forecast GtG_{t} for all t∈[N]t\in[N]. Consequently, the parameter-estimation error satisfies

where the bounding zonotope is known a priori, without requiring future measurements. This allows the controller to anticipate guaranteed future parameter uncertainty reduction during planning. Similarly, using (12)-(13), we can bound the parameter-estimate shift as follows:
